claim: Premise-wise majority voting over logically linked propositions can yield an inconsistent collective set (doctrinal paradox, discursive dilemma); conclusion-wise and premise-wise verdicts can differ on the same votes.
agent_test: Run N sampled answers with sub-claims; compare conclusion-vote vs premise-vote final answers at equal tokens; count disagreements and which is right.
audit_note: Minor: Grossi and Pigozzi is a tutorial recounting Kornhauser and Sager / Pettit, and List (2005) builds on the same paradox, so the sources are independent authors but the example is a single well-known result; nested wording (premise-wise vs conclusion-wise verdicts differ on the same votes) is shown by the three-judge example.

claim: Any aggregation rule on a rich agenda that is universal-domain and systematic is dictatorial (List-Pettit impossibility); relaxing a condition (for example unidimensional alignment) restores consistency.
agent_test: Declare which condition the agent drops (systematicity: premise-based rather than proposition-wise) and log it per task.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-01 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: The doctrinal paradox is not rare: for the conjunctive agenda inconsistency tends to 0.25 under impartial culture (n=101: 0.2500) and to 1 under mild departures (n=1501: 0.9999). Table re-verified in List 2005.
agent_test: Simulate on the agent's own sub-claim vote profiles; measure inconsistency rate.

claim: Premise-based voting tracks truth better than conclusion-based voting for independent competent voters (PBP tends to 1 when p,q>0.5), but can overturn a unanimous conclusion.
agent_test: Compare premise-first vs answer-first aggregation on multi-step problems at equal samples.
audit_note: Minor: List shows CBP can reach the correct decision faster than PBP when the premises are not both true, so 'tracks truth better' holds mainly when premises are true; the claim's PBP-to-1 statement is correct.

claim: For independent voters of equal competence p, majority accuracy rises toward 1 with group size if p>1/2; if p<1/2 it falls toward 0 and a single voter is best (Condorcet jury theorem).
agent_test: Estimate per-item p from sample agreement; do not vote when modal answer share is below a threshold.
audit_note: Condorcet theorem (Wikipedia, List 2008 for the >1/2 and independence conditions) is stated for equal-competence independent voters; 'only if' is too strong (heterogeneous competence, Berend-Paroush, and correlated cases are not covered), and List 2008 does not state the p<1/2 case.
claim_before_audit: Majority beats a single voter only if competence exceeds 1/2 and voters are independent; with competence below 1/2 more voters make it worse.

claim: LLM errors violate Condorcet independence: across 349 LLMs on 12,032 questions agreement when both wrong is 0.423 vs 0.127 chance (Helm about 0.60 vs 0.333); 100% of HF pairs above chance; more accurate models are more correlated. Re-verified in the paper.
agent_test: Measure wrong-wrong agreement among our N samples and across personas/prompts; effective N = N/(1+(N-1)rho).

claim: Repeated samples from one model are highly correlated: ICC 0.50-0.93, ten ratings worth 1.07-1.81 independent ones; independence models were overconfident in 42 of 42 settings.
agent_test: Estimate ICC on our own sampling; set sample count by effective N.
gap_search_note: Gap search: a second measurement, mean pairwise error correlation among 5 samples of gpt-oss-120b is 0.633 (GPQA) and 0.571 (LCB-Hard) with persona prompts, 0.603 and 0.607 with one prompt (d11). Design effect gives about 1.5 effective voters out of 5 (my arithmetic). Still one team per number; status kept.

claim: Self-consistency (plain majority over sampled chains) gives large gains: GSM8K +17.9, SVAMP +11.0, AQuA +12.2, StrategyQA +6.4, ARC-c +3.9 (PaLM-540B), verified. Plain vote is about as good as normalised probability-weighted vote; unnormalised weighting was worse (59.9 vs 74.1 on GSM8K).
agent_test: Baseline vs majority at 5, 10, 20 samples; compare weighted vs plain.

claim: Sampling-and-voting scales with the number of agents and a small model with votes can pass a larger single model (Llama2-13B ensemble 59% vs 70B single 54% on GSM8K).
agent_test: Compare small-model-with-votes against a single larger call at equal tokens.

claim: Majority vote saturates while coverage keeps rising: MATH Llama-3-8B coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000, vote only 40.50% to 41.41%; verifier-based selection lifts SWE-bench Lite 15.9% to 56% at 250 samples. Verified.
agent_test: Where a checker exists, select by checker not vote; measure the coverage-vs-vote gap.
gap_search_note: Gap search: outside code and math, a 33-verifier weighted ensemble (Weaver) lifted a 70B generator from 72.2 (vote) to 87.7 average, GPQA about 47 to 72, but needed a labelled dev set and a plain average of verifiers did not beat the vote (d19). False positives of a weak verifier cap the gain and make the best sample count small (K about 5 in code, d20).

claim: Per-query competence can fall below 1/2 on hard items, so majority-vote accuracy can rise then fall with more calls (the modal answer on a hard query is wrong).
agent_test: Bin items by agreement; test whether extra samples hurt on low-agreement items.
gap_search_note: Gap search: agreement share correlates with accuracy (d04) and is safe as a stopping rule (d02, d03), but nobody tested it as an abstain gate or measured where per-item competence drops below 1/2.

claim: Most of the gain from multi-agent debate is reproduced by majority voting; debate alone is a martingale. Qwen2.5-7B 7-benchmark mean: single 0.7205, debate T=2 0.7377, T=5 0.7050, centralised 0.6551, vote 0.7691 (verified).
agent_test: Compare vote vs debate at equal tokens; default to vote.
gap_search_note: Gap search: two more equal-budget tests agree. Token-budget study (GPT-3.5/4): debate 6x3=18 queries lost to CoT-SC 20 and declined with budget (d13). 23 small models, 5,500 runs: solo 80.4, debate 84.4, SC-9 84.8; debate cost 3.4x tokens (d14). Mixed-model teams lost to majority over their own roster by 1.04 points.

claim: Debate can beat single agent and simple majority in some settings (Du 2023: arithmetic 81.8 vs majority 69.0; MMLU 63.9 to 71.1), but results depend on baseline prompt strength and tuning.
agent_test: Re-run a debate arm against a strong single-prompt baseline at equal tokens.

claim: Heterogeneous model panels judge better and with less self-bias than one big judge (PoLL: Pearson 0.917 vs 0.817; kappa 0.763 vs 0.627 on NQ); deliberation helps mixed-family groups but not clones.
agent_test: Not testable with one model; test persona/prompt diversity as the proxy and measure error correlation.
audit_note: Pearson/Kendall figures are from Chatbot Arena agreement, kappa from NQ; both match PoLL paper; deliberation abstract (2609.22497) confirms diversity needed, clones no benefit.

claim: Mixing different models is not always better than repeating the best one (Self-MoA +6.6 AlpacaEval, +3.8 average); this contradicts the MoA claim that mixing helps.
agent_test: With one model diversity comes only from prompts; test whether prompt diversity beats repeat sampling at equal tokens.
gap_search_note: Gap search: d14 found mixed-model teams lose to a majority vote over their own roster (-1.04 points, 80 teams), accuracy tracking member capability, not heterogeneity. Supports Self-MoA side. Still contested versus MoA.

claim: A model acting as aggregator is not better than a code rule: USC 0.1691 vs trimmed mean 0.1649 and no ensemble 0.1676 (verified); a GPT-4o flip judge gave net -1.37%.
agent_test: Aggregate in code; compare with an LLM merge step at equal tokens.
gap_search_note: Gap search: downgraded from established. On reasoning tasks an LLM that reads full traces beat vote at about equal calls (SC-MoA BBH 86.5 vs SC 80.4; AIME 91.1 vs 85.6; LCB-Hard 62.6 vs 57.3, d10), and USC matches exact-match vote where both apply (d18). The earlier result (forecast probabilities, flip judge) still holds for numeric aggregation. Aggregator type depends on task.

claim: For probability forecasts simple aggregation is hard to beat: trimmed mean 0.1649, mean 0.1656, median 0.1651, geometric 0.1655 (verified, tiny differences). Extremizing helps when forecasters hold different information (GJP superforecasters Brier 0.132 mean, 0.128 log-odds, 0.123 model).
agent_test: Compare mean, median, trimmed mean, log-odds mean on our confidence outputs; extremize only if samples are diverse.

claim: A crowd of 12 LLMs (median) matched a 925-human crowd on 31 questions (Brier 0.20 vs 0.19, p=0.850, verified) with acquiescence bias; averaging with humans beat letting the model update.
agent_test: Small-N result; replicate with the agent's own forecasts on resolved post-cutoff questions.

claim: LLM forecasters still trail superforecasters (0.096 vs best LLM 0.122) and averaging system plus crowd beats either alone.
agent_test: Calibration check at S8; not a design lever.
audit_note: Minor: Halawi's aggregate is a weighted average (4x weight on crowd), not a plain average.

claim: Humans: pooling independent doctors beat the best member only when accuracies were similar (gap below 0.1); social influence cut diversity (Lorenz) though decentralised networks still raised accuracy (Becker).
agent_test: Keep samples blind to each other before voting; test shown-others vs blind at equal tokens.
gap_search_note: Gap search: Kurvers 2016 and Lorenz 2011 reopened from PMC full text. Kurvers: 101 radiologists / 182 mammograms / 16,813 diagnoses and 40 dermatologists / 108 lesions / 4,320 diagnoses; pooling beat the best member only when |delta J| < 0.1 (d06). Lorenz: N=144, 21.3% figure confirmed (arithmetic mean closer than individual first estimates); in log space 77.1% (d07). Becker 2017 still not reopened, so status stays contested.

claim: Confidence-weighted pooling with some self-weight helped in LLM networks, but a trained flip rule recovered little of the oracle margin (10.0 points margin, +1.71 net).
agent_test: Confidence-weighted vs plain vote at equal samples.
gap_search_note: Gap search: confidence weighting helps when the signal ranks right vs wrong samples of one question (CISC: 41% to 46% fewer samples for P(True), accuracy gain 1 to 2 points, d01) and hurts or is useless otherwise (Qwen3-1.7B P(True) AUROC 0.47, d05; Wang 2023 unnormalised weights worse). The sign depends on the confidence signal and the model.

claim: Bagging three correlated classifiers added almost nothing (F1 -0.01), consistent with failed independence.
agent_test: Same as K06.

claim: Voting rules did better on reasoning tasks, consensus rules on knowledge tasks; more agents helped, more discussion rounds hurt.
agent_test: Task-type switch between vote and consensus; measure.

claim: Cross-question consistency checks (negation, conditional) correlate with Brier, but forcing consistency did not improve accuracy.
agent_test: Use consistency as a diagnostic, not a repair.

claim: Training-cutoff leakage inflates LLM forecasting aggregates: cloud vs local mean Brier gap 35.8% on the full set vs 8.9% on the clean subset.
agent_test: Use only post-cutoff questions in any agent test.

claim: Persona or paraphrase prompts do not reduce error correlation among samples from one model: about 0.6 in both cases on GPQA-Diamond and LCB-Hard (N=5, gpt-oss-120b); persona prompts lowered accuracy in 23 small models.
agent_test: Estimate pairwise error correlation on our own sampling with and without prompt variants; set the sample count from n_eff, not n.

claim: Agreement-based early stopping cuts samples roughly 1.5x to 8x (Adaptive-Consistency: 3.3x on math on average, up to 7.9x, GPT-3.5 4.4x, with under 0.1% average accuracy drop; ESC: -34% to -84% samples with comparable accuracy). It measures lead stability, not correctness.
agent_test: Add a stopping rule to the vote; log accuracy by final lead; do not treat a stable lead as proof.
audit_note: Adaptive-Consistency reports 3.3x average (up to 7.9x) with under 0.1% average accuracy drop, but ESC's -33.8% (MATH) is only about 1.5x and ESC reports only 'comparable' accuracy, so '2x to 8x with under 0.1 point loss' for both is wider than the sources.
claim_before_audit: Agreement-based stopping cuts samples 2x to 8x with under 0.1 point average accuracy loss on reasoning tasks (Adaptive-Consistency: math 3.3x fewer, GPT-3.5 4.4x; ESC: -34% to -84%). It measures lead stability, not correctness.

claim: Confidence-informed voting from one model's own samples saves 41% to 46% of samples at P(True) weights with within-question softmax normalisation; verbal confidence saves 10% to 30%. The best-calibrated confidence was not the best weight.
agent_test: Compare plain vote, verbal-confidence weighted vote and P(True) weighted vote at equal samples on our tasks; judge confidence by within-question ranking.

claim: Outside code and math, verifier ensembles can beat majority vote (Weaver: 87.7 vs about 72 average; GPQA about 47 to 72) but only as a labelled-data weighted ensemble of many verifiers; a plain average did not help. A weak verifier's false positives cap resampling gains and the best K is often about 5.
agent_test: Use a real checker (tool, test, retrieval). Treat same-model self-verification as a weak verifier; log false positives and cap the sample count.
audit_note: Minor: Weaver's 87.7 average includes MATH500, so 'outside code and math' strictly applies to the GPQA/MMLU entries; Stroebl's K about 5 is for code with a false-positive cost ratio of 4, and Weaver's majority baseline varies 71.6-72.2 across tables.

claim: Debate versus vote at matched budget: debate is a mild gain over one answer (+3 to +7 points) but ties or loses to independent-sample majority vote and costs 1.6x wall-clock and 3.4x tokens; discussion's gain shrinks as agents withhold dissent, and it can overturn a wrong majority only when withholding is below a critical rate.
agent_test: Default to independent samples plus vote; add discussion only after an equal-token test shows a gain.
audit_note: Ferreira et al. and Wang et al. support the numbers (+3.3/+6.6/+5.7, 1.6x, 3.4x), but Mansuri et al. show discussion's gain shrinks as dissent withholding rises and can overturn a wrong majority only below a critical withholding rate, not that discussion helps 'only if' dissent is voiced.
claim_before_audit: Debate versus vote at matched budget: debate is a mild gain over one answer (+3 to +7 points) but ties or loses to independent-sample majority vote and costs 1.6x wall-clock and 3.4x tokens; discussion helps only if dissent is voiced.

claim: Varying the method named in the prompt (not only the temperature) can lift hard planning tasks a lot (graph colouring 23 -> 97 on GPT-4), but persona diversity did not lower error correlation or raise accuracy elsewhere, so part of the gain is better prompts, not independence.
agent_test: Compare temperature-only samples, method-prompt samples and persona samples at equal tokens, and report error correlation for each.

claim: Default extremizing factor for samples from one model should be 1 (none): extremizing is justified when forecasters have private information, and with shared information the right move can be to anti-extremize. No LLM-sample test exists.
agent_test: Fit a log-odds aggregator with extremizing factor as a free parameter on held-out agent probabilities; expect a factor at or below 1.

claim: Flipping to the minority is risky: always trusting the minority costs 19 points, a trained flip rule in a 3-vendor debate recovers 22% of the minority-correct cases (39 of 175) for a net gain of only +1.71 points (about 17% of the 10-point oracle margin), and on one small model a label-free delegation rule adds 1.5 to 2.2 points (366 wins vs 185 losses). An LLM reconciler recovers minority-correct answers on math but with unreported harm counts.
agent_test: Allow a flip only through a tested gate; count right-to-wrong flips as well as wrong-to-right.
audit_note: Minority Sentinel's 22.3% is the recovery rate of minority-correct 2:1 cases (39 of 175), not 22% of the oracle margin (net +1.71 of a 10.0-point margin is about 17%); other numbers (-19.16, +1.5/+2.24, 366 vs 185) match.
claim_before_audit: Flipping to the minority is risky: blind trust costs 19 points, a trained flip rule in a 3-vendor debate recovers 22% of the oracle margin (+1.71), and on one small model a label-free delegation rule adds 1.5 to 2.2 points (366 wins vs 185 losses). An LLM reconciler recovers minority-correct answers on math but with unreported harm counts.

claim: For skewed numeric outputs the arithmetic mean is a poor aggregate (closer than individuals in only 21.3% of cases; 77.1% in log space); median or geometric mean was far closer to the truth. Earlier forecast work (Douven, clean set) found the mean beat the median, so the choice depends on the distribution.
agent_test: Check skew of the sample distribution; default to median or geometric mean for positive numbers and log-odds for probabilities.

claim: Reading sub-steps beats counting final answers on reasoning tasks at about equal calls (+6.1 on BBH-3, +5.5 on AIME, +5.3 on LCB-Hard), and final-answer votes are often right for wrong reasons (MedQA SC-only wins 40% faithful). No study has measured a doctrinal-paradox rate or premise-wise code voting on LLM samples.
agent_test: Build the premise-wise code vote and measure it against answer vote and an LLM trace reader at equal tokens; count samples whose sub-claims disagree with the conclusion.

claim: Surprisingly-popular aggregation has no published test on a single model's samples. Its premise (an informed minority) is absent in one model's samples, while LLMs do favour popular wrong options (66% when all distractors are more popular).
agent_test: Pilot: ask the model for its answer and its predicted share of other samples choosing each option; compare SP pick with modal pick at equal samples.
